sections.name: engineering
sections.label: Engineering
sections.intro: Coding agents matured with concrete cost numbers, alongside an LLM pinpointing an obscure bike-light battery part number.

stories.title: 2026 in LLMs (so far)
stories.summary: In November 2025, Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 made coding agents reliable enough for daily use. OpenClaw grew to over 100,000 commits by early 2026, defining a new class of consumer-facing coding agents called Claws. StrongDM's Dark Factory banned human-written and reviewed code, token costs rose from fifty to over a thousand dollars per day, and 40 of 277 conference sessions tackled agent sandboxing.
stories.why: It maps how coding agents matured in 2026 with concrete numbers on commits, costs, and open sandboxing problems.
stories.takeaway: Coding agents crossed a reliability threshold in late 2025, but the open problem is sandboxing: keeping them safe enough for non-technical users.

stories.title: Replacing the old battery on rechargeable bike lights
stories.summary: A beginner desoldered and replaced LIR2477 coin-cell batteries in 10-year-old bike lights for about $20 CAD in parts from AliExpress. An LLM decoded an unreadable battery marking after DigiKey's search couldn't locate the part. The project used an iFixit desoldering guide and a community makerspace.
stories.why: A concrete example of using an LLM to identify an obscure battery part number when standard supplier catalogs fail.
stories.takeaway: LLMs can identify obscure component markings when supplier catalogs fail, though the author notes better non-LLM methods likely exist.

stories.title: Human-AI partnerships are for alignment, not capability
stories.summary: AI coding agents write more correct code than humans, but their output is misaligned with organizational values: bloated comments, useless tests, ignored long-term strategy. The engineer's job is to align the AI to company-specific technical values, which are context-dependent and hard to train into models.
stories.why: Reframes the engineer-AI relationship: the human's value is technical judgment and context, not raw code quality.
stories.takeaway: Your moat as an engineer is knowing your system's context and tradeoffs, since AI already beats you at code.

sections.name: papers
sections.label: Papers
sections.intro: Two papers trace exactly-once delivery costs in stream engines and the failure modes it leaves inside LLM agent tool calls.

stories.title: Where Does Streaming State Cost Go? A Reproducible Comparison of Flink and Kafka Streams on Kafka
stories.summary: At 100 events per second, both engines stayed correct across 50 trials. Windowed workloads took 4.3 to 6.2 seconds end to end with p99 of 5.7 to 9.9 seconds, versus milliseconds when stateless. Raising the durability interval from 1s to 10s pushed Kafka Streams p99 from 6.1s to 23.2s on one stage and Flink from 0.7s to 8.7s on another, and failure injection surfaced incomplete processing only when latency spiked.
stories.why: Exactly-once streams sound safe, but latency and recovery cost differ sharply by engine architecture.
stories.takeaway: Correctness guarantees hide large latency gaps under state and durability pressure, so benchmark end to end before picking an engine.

stories.title: Where Does Exactly-Once Live? Model, Harness, and Tool-Contract Effects on Duplicate Side Effects in LLM Agents
stories.summary: LIMBO is a sandbox of six services with 12 fault modes grading 25,930 agent episodes against an effect ledger. When a read-back can confirm a write, frontier models duplicate only 0.5%; when writes are in-flight or redelivered, even they duplicate 56-74%, and tool contracts explain 81% of variance. No verify-only policy achieves exactly-once under late commits without bounding in-flight time.
stories.why: Exactly-once delivery is a classic distributed systems problem; this paper maps where it fails inside LLM agent tool calls.
stories.takeaway: Exactly-once for agent tool calls lives in the model when read-backs work, in the tool contract when they cannot.

sections.name: tools
sections.label: Tools
sections.intro: DSPy ports to the BEAM as supervised OTP processes, and a neural audio model runs on an ESP32 within hard real-time budgets.

stories.title: Imp is a full port of DSPy to the BEAM
stories.summary: Imp ports DSPy's signatures, modules, optimizers (GEPA, MIPROv2, SIMBA, few-shot, fine-tuning) and agent loops to Elixir. Agents run as supervised OTP processes with deadlines, per-call tool authorization, and an event stream; tool calls that may have side effects are reported as unknown rather than silently retried. Version 0.5 is experimental, MIT-licensed, and needs Elixir 1.19 plus a C/C++ toolchain.
stories.why: DSPy is now on the BEAM, giving Elixir engineers typed, optimizable LM programs that run as supervised OTP processes.
stories.takeaway: LM workflows gain OTP-style supervision: every run is a process you can watch, kill, and authorize, with no silent retries on side-effecting tool calls.

stories.title: Guitar amp and effects pedal built on the Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-2.06
stories.summary: CoyoPedal runs a 23-layer, eight-channel WaveNet NAM A2 model at 48 kHz on an ESP32-S3, using hand-written Xtensa kernels with block floating point split across both cores. It hits 91% and 94 percent of a 1333 microsecond block budget per core with no missed deadlines, while a TSX UI compiles to native C++ and the same firmware also builds to WebAssembly.
stories.why: A real-world case study of running a neural audio model on a microcontroller under hard real-time budgets.
stories.takeaway: Modern neural audio fits on constrained MCUs when numerics, kernels and block scheduling are chosen deliberately.

sections.name: discussions
sections.label: Discussions
sections.intro: S3's disk-era latency shapes modern data architectures, and a free local emulator offers a LocalStack alternative for AWS integration tests.

stories.title: S3 Is the Future, S3 Is the Past
stories.summary: S3 imposes an architectural tax: caching layers, write batching, separate metadata stores like DynamoDB or FoundationDB, and full-object rewrites all work around its disk-derived constraints. Modern SSDs deliver around 100 microsecond latency and millions of IOPS near disk prices; 100+ Gbit networks add sub-100-microsecond intra-DC latency. Cloud providers will not disrupt their revenue, so engineers should build SSD-native primitives themselves.
stories.why: S3's disk-era latency and per-request bandwidth shape every modern data architecture, but SSDs and fast networks have outgrown them.
stories.takeaway: Today's S3-centric patterns are workarounds for hardware constraints that no longer exist; build storage assuming microsecond SSD latency.
stories.debate: Commenters split on whether S3 is actually cheap or merely convenient, with one noting six months of S3 equals buying a 4TB SSD outright. Others argue current cloud SSD pricing still forces S3 use at big-data scale.

stories.title: Fakecloud: Local AWS cloud emulator for integration tests
stories.summary: fakecloud emulates 105 AWS services and 3,932 API operations, claiming 248,557 Smithy test variants pass. It runs as a single binary or Docker image, accepts any dummy creds, and provides first-party SDKs for inspecting SES emails, SQS messages, and Lambda invocations after normal AWS SDK calls.
stories.why: Local AWS emulator alternative to LocalStack that needs no auth or paid tier for testing real AWS client code locally.
stories.takeaway: When evaluating cloud emulators, verify conformance claims independently and weigh trust signals against convenient features.
stories.debate: Commenters dispute the 100 percent conformance claim, noting incomplete DynamoDB behavior, and question whether external simulators beat inline test mocking. Others raise trust concerns about anonymous authors and a curl-to-shell installer.
